label: IntroAPS
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{IntroAPS}
  Let $\overline{\Omega}$ be an even-dimensional spin manifold with boundary, which carries a free, proper, isometric action by the discrete group $\Gamma$. Suppose that the metric on $\overline{\Omega}$ is collared, and that the boundary has uniformly positive scalar curvature. Then,
  $$
    \mathrm{Ind}_\mathrm{sec}^\Gamma(\slashed{D}_\Omega) = \mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_\mathrm{APS}(\slashed{D}_\Omega) + \rho^\Gamma(\slashed{D}_{\partial\Omega}) \; .
  $$
head: environment

label: IntroTransform
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Let $D^*(X)^\Gamma$ denote the $C^*$-algebra generated by all pseudo-local $\Gamma$-invariant finite-propagation operators. Let $D^*(X,Z)^\Gamma$ denote the $C^*$-algebra generated by all pseudo-local $\Gamma$-invariant finite-propagation operators that are locally compact over $X\setminus Z$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Define $D^*(A\subseteq X,Z)^\Gamma$ as the $C^*$-algebra generated by all pseudo-local $\Gamma$-invariant finite-propagation operators that are supported near $A$ and locally compact over $X\setminus Z$.
head: environment

label: RoeIncl
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{RoeIncl}
  The inclusion $A\hookrightarrow X$ induces an isomorphism
  $$
    K_*\left( C^*(A)^\Gamma \right) \xlongrightarrow{\sim} K_*\left( C^*(A\subseteq X)^\Gamma \right) \; .
  $$
head: environment

label: TrivialKtheory
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{TrivialKtheory}
  $K_*(\mathfrak{C}(X)^\Gamma)=0$\; .
head: environment

label: StructureDual
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{StructureDual} 
  Suppose that $Z\subseteq A$. Then,
  $$
  \frac{D^*(A \subseteq X, Z)^\Gamma}{C^*(A \subseteq X)^\Gamma} = \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X, Z)^\Gamma}{\mathfrak{C}(X)^\Gamma}\; .
  $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The properties of the truncation map \eqref{TruncMap} together with use of a cut-off function yield that $\mathfrak{D}(X, Z)^\Gamma = D^*(A \subseteq X, Z)^\Gamma + \mathfrak{C}(X)^\Gamma$, giving one inclusion. The observation that $C^*(A\subseteq X)^\Gamma$ equals the intersection of $D^*(A \subseteq X, Z)^\Gamma$ and $\mathfrak{C}(X)^\Gamma$ gives the reverse inclusion.
head: environment

label: RelQuot
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{RelQuot}
  It holds that
  $$
  \frac{D^*(X)^\Gamma}{D^*(X,Z)^\Gamma} = \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X)^\Gamma}{\mathfrak{D}(X,Z)^\Gamma}\; .
  $$
head: environment

label: EquivQuotient
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{EquivQuotient}
  There is an isomorphism 
  $$
  \frac{D^*(A\subseteq X,Z)^\Gamma}{C^*(A\subseteq X)^\Gamma} \cong \frac{D^*(A_\Gamma\subseteq X_\Gamma, Z_\Gamma)}{C^*(A_\Gamma \subseteq X_\Gamma)} \; .
  $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Pick a locally finite cover of $X_\Gamma$ by open sets $U_i$ with uniformly bounded diameters such that the pre-image $\tilde{U}_i$ of $U_i$ in $X$ is isomorphic to $U_i \times \Gamma$. Any operator over $X_\Gamma$ with support in $U_i\times U_i$ can then be lifted to a $\Gamma$-equivariant operator over $X$ with support in $\tilde{U}_i \times \tilde{U}_i$. Conversely, any such operator over $X$ arises from a unique operator over $X_\Gamma$ in this way. This procedure preserves the properties of being pseudo-local, being supported near $A$ or $A_\Gamma$, and being locally compact on the complement of $Z$ or $Z_\Gamma$. Finally, the truncation map \eqref{TruncMap} can be used to represent a class in either quotient by the strong limit of a series of operators with supports in some $U_i$ or $\tilde{U}_i$, respectively. For the details we refer to the discussion around Theorem 4.3.25 in \cite{Siegel2012}.
head: environment

label: RelLocalized
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{RelLocalized}
  Suppose that $Z\subseteq A$. Then, the inclusion $A\hookrightarrow X$ induces an isomorphism
  $$
  K_*\left( D^*(A,Z)^\Gamma \right) \xlongrightarrow{\sim} K_*\left( D^*(A\subseteq X,Z)^\Gamma \right) \; .
  $$
head: environment

title: Proof

title: Corollary

\label{RelLocalizedAisZ}
  The inclusion $Z\hookrightarrow X$ induces an isomorphism
  $$
  K_*\left( D^*(Z)^\Gamma \right) \xlongrightarrow{\sim} K_*\left( D^*(Z\subseteq X,Z)^\Gamma \right) \; .

label: IsoRelBdry
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{IsoRelBdry}
  Suppose that $N_c(Z)=X$ for some $c\geq 0$. Then, the inclusion $Z\hookrightarrow X$ induces an isomorphism
  $$
  K_*\left( D^*(Z)^\Gamma \right) \xlongrightarrow{\sim} K_*\left( D^*(X,Z)^\Gamma \right) \; .
  $$

label: AlgebraicMV
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Using cutoff functions one shows that the algebra $D^*(X,Z)^\Gamma$ can be written as $D^*(X,Z)^\Gamma=C^*(X)^\Gamma + D^*(Z\subseteq X,Z)^\Gamma$. Both summands are closed two-sided $^*$-ideals, and their intersection is given by $C^*(Z\subseteq X)^\Gamma$. Application of \cref{RoeIncl} and \cref{RelLocalized} to the corresponding Mayer-Vietoris sequence on K-theory concludes the proof.
head: environment

label: CoarseEqMV
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{CoarseEqMV}
  The algebraic Mayer-Vietoris sequence allows us to extend the conclusion of \cref{IsoRelBdry} to the case where $Z$ is coarsely equivalent to $X$, but not necessarily $c$-dense. Indeed, if $Z\hookrightarrow X$ is a coarse equivalence of $\Gamma$-spaces, the map $K_*(C^*(Z)^\Gamma) \to K_*(C^*(X)^\Gamma)$ is an isomorphism. From the Mayer-Vietoris sequence one may then deduce that $K_*(D^*(Z)^\Gamma)\to K_*(D^*(X,Z)^\Gamma)$ is an isomorphism, and that the boundary map $\delta: \,K_*(D^*(X,Z)^\Gamma) \to K_{*-1}(C^*(Z)^\Gamma)$ is zero. The latter fact is a version of bordism invariance of the index, see \cref{BordInvIndex} below.
head: environment

label: EquivKhom
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Ad (i): It holds that 
  $$
    K^\Gamma_*(X,Z) \cong K_{*+1}\left( \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X)^\Gamma}{\mathfrak{D}(X,Z)^\Gamma} \right) = K_{*+1}\left( \frac{D^*(X)^\Gamma}{D^*(X,Z)^\Gamma} \right) \; ,
  $$
  where the first (natural) isomorphism is due to Paschke duality (see e.g. \cite{Higson1995} for the non-equivariant case), and the second equality is due to \cref{RelQuot}.
  
  Ad (ii): Combine \cref{StructureDual} and \cref{EquivQuotient} to see that 
  $$
    \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X,Z)^\Gamma}{\mathfrak{C}(X)^\Gamma} = \frac{D^*(X,Z)^\Gamma}{C^*(X)^\Gamma} \cong \frac{D^*(X_\Gamma,Z_\Gamma)}{C^*(X_\Gamma)} = \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma,Z_\Gamma)}{\mathfrak{C}(X_\Gamma)} \; .
  $$
  Analogously, one finds that $\mathfrak{D}(X)^\Gamma/\mathfrak{C}(X)^\Gamma \cong \mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma)/\mathfrak{C}(X_\Gamma)$. These isomorphisms fit into the larger diagram \\
  \centerline{\xymatrix{
    0 \ar[r] &  \mathfrak{D}(X,Z)^\Gamma \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathfrak{D}(X)^\Gamma \ar[r] \ar[d] & \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X)^\Gamma}{\mathfrak{D}(X,Z)^\Gamma} \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\
    0 \ar[r] &  \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X,Z)^\Gamma}{\mathfrak{C}(X)^\Gamma} \ar[r] \ar[d]_\sim & \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X)^\Gamma}{\mathfrak{C}(X)^\Gamma} \ar[r]\ar[d]_\sim & Q(X,Z)^\Gamma \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\
    0 \ar[r] &  \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma,Z_\Gamma)}{\mathfrak{C}(X_\Gamma)} \ar[r] & \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma)}{\mathfrak{C}(X_\Gamma)} \ar[r] & Q(X_\Gamma,Z_\Gamma) \ar[r] & 0 \\
    0 \ar[r] &  \mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma,Z_\Gamma) \ar[r] \ar[u] & \mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma) \ar[r] \ar[u] & \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma)}{\mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma,Z_\Gamma)}\ar[r] \ar[u] & 0
  }}
  where $Q(X,Z)^\Gamma$ and $Q(X_\Gamma,Z_\Gamma)$ denote the appropriate quotient algebras. Commutativity of the middle squares holds because all middle arrows are defined via the same quotienting/lifting procedure described in the proof of \cref{EquivQuotient}. By \cref{TrivialKtheory} the upper- and lower-left, and upper- and lower-middle arrows are K-theory isomorphisms. Hence, upon passing to the corresponding diagram between long exact K-theory sequences, we obtain isomorphisms
  $$
    K_*(\mathfrak{D}(X,Z)^\Gamma) \cong K_*(\mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma,Z_\Gamma)) \quad , \quad K_*(\mathfrak{D}(X)^\Gamma) \cong K_*(\mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma))
  $$
  The Five lemma lets us conclude
  $$
    K_*^\Gamma(X,Z) \cong K_{*+1}\left( \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X)^\Gamma}{\mathfrak{D}(X,Z)^\Gamma} \right) \cong K_{*+1}\left( \frac{\mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma)}{\mathfrak{D}(X_\Gamma,Z_\Gamma)} \right) \cong K_*(X_\Gamma,Z_\Gamma) \; .
  $$
  Compatibility with the boundary maps follows from the fact that the K-theory boundary map is natural with respect to maps of short exact seuquences.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The \emph{secondary index map} is defined as the composition
  $$
  \mathrm{Ind}_\mathrm{sec}^\Gamma: \; K_*^\Gamma(X,Z) \cong K_{*+1}\left( \frac{D^*(X)^\Gamma}{D^*(X,Z)^\Gamma} \right) \xlongrightarrow{\partial} K_*(D(X,Z)^\Gamma) \; .
  $$
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
As a consequence of \cref{EquivKhom} (ii), one could in principle forego equivariant K-homology, and work with the pair $(X_\Gamma, Z_\Gamma)$ together with the datum of a locally isometric $\Gamma$-covering determining $(X,Z)$: Suppose for the sake of concreteness that $\overline{\Omega}$ is a complete riemannian manifold with boundary. Associated to any continuous map $f: \, \overline{\Omega} \to B\Gamma$ to the classifying space of $\Gamma$, there is an associated $\Gamma$-covering $X\to \overline{\Omega}$. Equip the total space $X$ with the pullback metric, and the $\Gamma$-action by deck transformations. Let $Z$ denote the pre-image of $\partial\Omega$ in $X$. Then $X_\Gamma = \overline{\Omega}$ and $Z_\Gamma = \partial\Omega$. In this situation, one may consider the secondary index map
  $$
    \mathrm{Ind}_\mathrm{sec}^\Gamma(f): \; K_*(\overline{\Omega},\partial\Omega) \cong K_*^\Gamma(X,Z) \xlongrightarrow{\mathrm{Ind}_\mathrm{sec}^\Gamma} K_*(D(X,Z)^\Gamma)
  $$
  with domain the (non-equivariant) K-homology of $(\overline{\Omega},\partial\Omega)$, which takes the classifying map $f$ as an additional datum. This approach has its own advantages, especially if it is the base space $\overline{\Omega}$ which is of primary geometric interest. Nevertheless, for our purposes we find it cleanest to work on the total space directly.

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $\overline{\Omega}$ be an even-dimensional, complete spin manifold with boundary. Suppose that $\overline{\Omega}$ carries a free, proper action of $\Gamma$ by spin isometries. Let $\chi$ be any normalizing function\footnote{A normalizing function is an odd, continuous function $\chi: \, \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty} \chi(\lambda)=1$.}. Then, the triple
  $$
    \left( L^2(\overline{\Omega}), \rho, \chi(\slashed{D}_e) \right)
  $$
  is a relative equivariant Fredholm module over $(\overline{\Omega},\partial\Omega)$, whose K-homology class is independent of $\chi$, and coincides with $[\slashed{D}] \in K^\Gamma_0(\Omega)$ under the excision isomorphism.

label: InvolutionModBdry
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{InvolutionModBdry}
  Suppose that $\overline{\Omega}$ has uniformly positive scalar curvature. Then, $\chi(\slashed{D}_e)$ is in $D^*(\overline{\Omega})^\Gamma$, and an involution modulo $D^*(\partial\Omega\subseteq \overline{\Omega},\partial\Omega)^\Gamma$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The proof is analogous to the boundaryless case (see e.g. \cite[Section~2]{Roe2016}). This is sketched in \cite[Remark~6.16]{Engel2026} (see also preceeding results therein), and details are given in the uniform setting in \cite[Section~7.1]{LykoThesis}.
head: environment

label: rem_psc_subset
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem_psc_subset}
  \cref{InvolutionModBdry} is analogous to the fact that if $M$ is a complete spin manifold without boundary that has upsc outside a subset $Z$, then $\chi(\slashed{D}_M)$ is an involution modulo $C^*(Z\subseteq M)$, see e.g. \cite[Section~2]{Roe2016}. Since $\slashed{D}^+_{\max}$ may have non-trivial kernel even in the presence of upsc, the boundary has to be treated as if it did not have positive scalar curvature. Indeed, \cref{InvolutionModBdry} can be straight-forwardly generalized to the situation where $\overline{\Omega}$ only has upsc outside some closed $Z\subseteq\overline{\Omega}$, in which case $\chi(\slashed{D}_e)$ is an involution modulo $D^*(\partial\Omega\cup Z \subseteq \overline{\Omega},\partial\Omega)$. We will not need this, however.

title: Definition
body_md: The \emph{higher $\rho$-invariant} $\rho^\Gamma(\slashed{D}_\Sigma)$ is defined as the class of $P_>$ in $K_0(D^*(\Sigma)^\Gamma)$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The \emph{delocalized APS-index} $\mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_\mathrm{APS}(\slashed{D}_\Omega)$ is defined as the image of $[\chi(\slashed{D}_M)]$ under the boundary map
    $$
      K_1\left(\frac{D^*(M)^\Gamma}{C^*(\overline{\Omega}\subseteq M)^\Gamma}\right) \xlongrightarrow{\partial} K_0\left( C^*(\overline{\Omega}\subseteq M)^\Gamma \right) \cong K_0\left( C^*(\overline{\Omega})^\Gamma \right) \; .
    $$
head: environment

label: RelIndRho
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $\overline{\Omega}$ be as in \cref{RelIndRho}.
  \begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] If $\overline{\Omega}$ has uniformly positive scalar curvature, then
    $$
      \rho^\Gamma(\slashed{D}_{\partial\Omega}) = 0 \; \in \; K_{0}\left( D^*(\overline{\Omega})^\Gamma\right) \; .
    $$
    \item[(ii)] If $\overline{\Omega}$ only has uniformly positive scalar curvature near the boundary, then
    $$
      \mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_{APS}(\slashed{D}_\Omega) = - \rho(\slashed{D}_{\partial\Omega}) \; \in \; K_{0}\left( D^*(\overline{\Omega})^\Gamma\right) \; .
    $$
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The secondary index maps $\mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_{\partial\Omega}$ and $\mathrm{Ind}_\mathrm{sec}^\Gamma$ are defined as K-theoretic boundary maps on the quotient of $D^*(\overline{\Omega})^\Gamma$ by the respective ideal. By exactness, their images lie in the kernel of the respective inclusion maps into $K_0(D^*(\overline{\Omega})^\Gamma)$. Hence, $\mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_{\partial\Omega}(\slashed{D}_\Omega)$ and $\mathrm{Ind}_\mathrm{sec}^\Gamma(\slashed{D}_\Omega)$ vanish upon being pushed into $K_0(D^*(\overline{\Omega})^\Gamma)$, so that the claim follows from the respective formulas in \cref{RelIndRho}.

label: SignAPS
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{SignAPS}
  In other treatments, the delocalized APS-index theorem (\cite{Piazza2014,Xie2014,Zeidler2016}) does not have the sign that ours does. This is a consequence of a difference in choice of orientation. Indeed, in the other treatments of this theorem the orientation on $M$ is chosen such that the attached cylinder is positively oriented, meaning that the orientation on $\Omega$ is reversed. While this results in a sign-free delocalized APS-index theorem, it is the less natural choice from our point of view. Since our primary interest was the relative index $\mathrm{Ind}_\mathrm{sec}^\Gamma(\slashed{D}_\Omega)$, it made sense for us to choose that orientation on $M$ which coincides with the given one on $\Omega$. This resulted in the sign.

label: KernelCylinder
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{KernelCylinder}
  Let $\Sigma$ be an odd-dimensional complete spin manifold with uniformly positive scalar curvature. Consider the operator $D = \partial_t + \slashed{D}_\Sigma$ on the cylinder $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times \Sigma$. It holds that
  $$
    \ker(D_{\max}) = \left\{ u(t,x) = e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 \, | \, u_0\in P_>L^2(\Sigma) \right\} \; .
  $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have to find all $u\in L^2(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times\Sigma)$ such that $(\partial_t + \slashed{D}_\Sigma)u=0$ in the sense of distributions. Due to interior regularity for the elliptic operator $D=\partial_t + \slashed{D}_\Sigma$, any such $u$ must be smooth in the interior. From this, one finds $u_t = u(t,-)$ to be a well-defined element of $\mathrm{dom}(\slashed{D}_\Sigma)$ for all $t>0$. We wish to check that the limit $u_0:=\lim_{t\to 0}u_t$ exists. Once this is done, standard results on Cauchy problems in Hilbert spaces (see e.g. \cite[~Prop. 6.6]{Schmudgen2012}) yield that $u_t = e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0$, which can only be square-integrable if $P_<u_0=0$.

  Existence of the $L^2$-limit can likely be derived from standard trace theorems (e.g. \cite[~Chapter 1]{Lions1972}). However, we will take a more pedestrian approach making use of the spectral gap for $\slashed{D}_\Sigma$. To that end, observe that 
  $$
    \frac{d}{dt} \| P_< u_t \|^2 = - 2 \langle P_< u_t, \slashed{D}_\Sigma P_< u_t \rangle \geq 2c \|P_< u_t\|^2 \; ,
  $$
  where we used $|\slashed{D}_\Sigma|\geq c>0$. Hence, $\| P_< u_t \|^2$ is a non-decreasing function for $t>0$. Since $u$ is square-integrable, this can only be if $P_<u_t = 0$ for all $t>0$. Hence, 
  $$
    \frac{d}{dt} \| u_t \|^2 = - 2 \langle u_t, \slashed{D}_\Sigma u_t \rangle \leq -2c \|u_t\|^2 \; .
  $$
  It follows that $\|u_t\|^2$ has a finite limit as $t\to 0$: Since $\|u_t\|^2$ is non-increasing, it suffices to show that $\|u_t\|^2$ is bounded for $t\to 0$. Fix some $t_0 > 0$. Then,
  $$
    \|u_t\|^2- \|u_{t_0}\|^2  =  -\int_{t}^{t_0} \frac{d\|u_s\|^2}{ds} \, ds  \leq 2c \int_t^{t_0} \|u_s\|^2 \, ds  \leq 2c\|u\|^2 < \infty \; ,
  $$
  where Tonelli's theorem justifies the final estimate. This proves boundedness.
  
  We use this to show that $u_t$, $t>0$, is a Cauchy net. Let $t>s>0$. It holds that $u_t = e^{-(t-s)\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_s$, from which we may conclude that $\langle u_t, u_s \rangle = \|u_{\frac{t-s}{2}}\|^2$. Thus
  $$
    \|u_t - u_s\|^2 = \|u_t\|^2 - 2\|u_{\frac{t-s}{2}}\|^2 + \|u_s\|^2 \xrightarrow{t,s\to 0} 0\; .
  $$
  Hence, the limit $u_0 = \lim_{t\to 0}u_t$ exists, which, as discussed above, completes the proof.
head: environment

label: FormulaCylinder
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{FormulaCylinder}
  Let $\Sigma$ be an odd-dimensional complete spin manifold with a free, proper, isometric $\Gamma$-action and uniformly positive scalar curvature. Consider $\overline{C}:= \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\times \Sigma$ with the product metric, and slice-wise $\Gamma$-action. Then,
  $$
    \mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_{\Sigma}(\slashed{D}_C) = \rho^\Gamma(\slashed{D}_{\Sigma}) \; \in \; K_{0}\left( D^*(\Sigma)^\Gamma\right) \; .
  $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As described in \cref{SectionBVPs}, the relative K-homology class of 
  $$
    \slashed{D}_\Omega = \slashed{D} = \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & \slashed{D}^- \\ \slashed{D}^+ & 0
    \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & -\partial_t + \slashed{D}_\Sigma \\ \partial_t + \slashed{D}_\Sigma & 0
    \end{pmatrix}
  $$ 
  can be obtained from the boundary condition
  $$
    \slashed{D}_e = \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & \slashed{D}^-_{\min} \\ \slashed{D}_{\max}^+ & 0
    \end{pmatrix} \; .
  $$
  Indeed, by assumption of upsc for $\Sigma$ (and hence also for $\overline{C}$), there is $c>0$ such that $\slashed{D}^+_{\max}\slashed{D}_{\min}^-\geq c^2$ and $\slashed{D}_\Sigma^2\geq c^2$. Pick a normalizing function $\chi$ such that $1-\chi^2$ is supported inside $(-c,c)$. Write $\chi(\slashed{D}_e)=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & U^* \\ U & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Then, 
  $$
    \begin{pmatrix}
    U^*U & 0 \\ 0 & UU^*
    \end{pmatrix} = \chi^2(\slashed{D}_e) = I - P_{\ker(\slashed{D}_e)} = \begin{pmatrix}
    I-P_{\ker(\slashed{D}^+_{\max})} & 0 \\ 0 & I
    \end{pmatrix}  \; .
  $$
  We conclude that $U$ is a partial isometry with kernel $\ker(\slashed{D}_{\max}^+)^\perp$ and trivial cokernel. Moreover, $I-\chi(\slashed{D}_e)^2 \in D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\overline{C},\Sigma)^\Gamma$, meaning that the projection $P_{\max}$ onto $\ker(\slashed{D}^+_{\max})$ is in $D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\overline{C},\Sigma)^\Gamma$. Indeed, the K-theory class $[P_{\max}] \in K_0(D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\overline{C},\Sigma)^\Gamma)$ represents the image of $[U] \in K_1(D^*(\overline{C})^\Gamma/D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\overline{C},\Sigma)^\Gamma)$ under the boundary map
  $$
    K_1\left(\frac{D^*(\overline{C})^\Gamma}{D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\overline{C},\Sigma)^\Gamma}\right) \xlongrightarrow{\partial} K_0\left(D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\overline{C},\Sigma)^\Gamma\right) \; .
  $$
  Up to the identifiction $K_0(D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\overline{C},\Sigma)^\Gamma)\cong K_0(D^*(\Sigma)^\Gamma)$ via \cref{RelLocalizedAisZ}, this boundary map is the secondary index map $\mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_\Sigma$. Since $P_>$ represents $\rho^\Gamma(\slashed{D}_\Sigma)$, we thus have to show that $[P_{\max}] = [P_{>}]$ under this identifiction. 
  
  In \cref{KernelCylinder} it was shown that $\ker(\slashed{D}_{\max}^+)=\ker((\partial_t + \slashed{D}_\Sigma)_{\max})$ consists precisely of $u\in L^2(\overline{C})$ with $u(t,-)=e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0$ and $u_0 \in P_>L^2(\Sigma)$. The remaining proof consists of turning this connection into an equality of K-theory classes. To that end, we shall first show that, up to homotopy, it suffices to consider the image of $P_{\max}$ up to some finite time $t=R$. Once this is done, we can homotope $t$ to zero, and identify the resulting projection with $P_>$.
  
  Fix some small $\varepsilon>0$. Because $P_{\max} \in D^*(\Sigma\subseteq \overline{C},\Sigma)^\Gamma$ is the limit of operators supported near $\Sigma$, there exists some $R\geq 0$ such that $\|P_{\max}u\|<\varepsilon\|u\|$ whenever $d(\mathrm{supp}(u),\Sigma) \geq R$. Then, let $P_R$ be the projection onto the subspace containing all functions $u(t,\cdot)=\psi_R\cdot e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0$ for $u_0\in P_>L^2(\Sigma)$, where $\psi_R=\mathbf{1}_{[0,R]}(t)$. Then 
  $$
    \|(P_{\max} - P^R)u\|=\|P_{\max}u\|<\varepsilon\|u\|
  $$
  if $d(\mathrm{supp}(u),\Sigma)\geq R$. Suppose on the other hand that $\mathrm{supp}(u)\subseteq [0,R]\times\Sigma$. Write $u=\psi_R e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 + u^\perp$, where $u^\perp$ is uniquely determined by the requirement that $\langle \psi_R e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma} v_0,u^\perp\rangle=0$ for all $v_0\in P_>L^2(\Sigma)$. Note that in particular $u^\perp=\psi_R u^\perp$, so that it follows that $\langle e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma} v_0,u^\perp\rangle=0$ for all $v_0\in P_>L^2(\Sigma)$ as well. Thus
  \begin{align*}
    \left\| (P_{\max} - P^R)u \right\| &= \left\| (P_{\max} - I)\psi_R e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 \right\| \\
    &= \left\| P_{\max} e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 - P_{\max}\left( (1-\psi_R)e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 \right) - \psi_R e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 \right\| \\
    &= \left\| e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 - P_{\max}\left( (1-\psi_R)e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 \right) - \psi_R e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 \right\| \\
    &\leq 2\cdot \left\| (1-\psi_R)e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 \right\| \; .
  \end{align*}
  It holds that 
  $$
  \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4} \int_{t=0}^R e^{-2t\lambda} \, dt \geq \int_{t=R}^\infty e^{-2t\lambda} \, dt
  $$
  for all $\lambda\geq c$ whenever $R$ is sufficiently large, say $R\gtrsim \log(\varepsilon^{-2}) c^{-1}$. Letting $E_\lambda$ denote the spectral measure of $\slashed{D}_\Sigma$, we go on to compute that
  \begin{align*}
  \left\| (1-\psi_R)e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 \right\|^2 &=  \int_{t=R}^\infty \left\| e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 \right\|^2 \, dt \\
  &= \int_{t=R}^\infty \left( \int_{\lambda=c}^\infty e^{-t\lambda} d\langle E_\lambda u_0,u_0\rangle \right) \, dt \\
  &= \int_{\lambda=c}^\infty \left( \int_{t=R}^\infty e^{-t\lambda}   \, dt \right) d\langle E_\lambda u_0,u_0\rangle \\
  &\leq \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4} \int_{\lambda=c}^\infty \left( \int_{t=0}^R e^{-t\lambda}   \, dt \right) d\langle E_\lambda u_0,u_0\rangle \\
  &= \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4} \left\| \psi_R e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0 \right\|^2 \\
  &\leq \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4} \|u\|^2 \; .
  \end{align*}
  The interchange of order of integration is justified by Tonelli's theorem. Thus
  $$
  \left\| (P_{\max} - P^R)u \right\| \leq \varepsilon \|u\| \; .
  $$
  Overall, we conclude that $P_{\max}$ and $P_R$ are projection whose difference has norm strictly less than $1$, so that they are homotopic (see for example \cite[Proposition 4.1.7]{HigsonRoe2000}).

  Let $\overline{C}_R=[0,R]\times \Sigma$, and denote by $V_R$ the inclusion map $L^2(\overline{C}_R)\hookrightarrow L^2(\overline{C})$. Also consider the isometry $V_\Sigma: \, L^2(\Sigma) \to L^2(\overline{C}_R)$, $(V_\Sigma v)(t,x)=R^{-1/2}v(x)$. The conjugation maps corresponding to these isometries induce the isomorphisms\footnote{More precisely, the isometry $V_\Sigma$ uniformly covers the inclusion $\Sigma \hookrightarrow [0,R]\times\Sigma$, and $V_R$ uniformly covers $[0,R]\times\Sigma \hookrightarrow \overline{C}$. For the sake of brevity, we have eschewed uniform covering isometries in our discussion of functoriality of (relative) structure algebras, so the reader is directed to \cite[~Section 4.3]{Siegel2012}.}
  $$
  K_*\left(D^*(\Sigma)^\Gamma \right) \xlongrightarrow{\sim} K_*\left( D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\overline{C}_R,\Sigma)^\Gamma \right) \xlongrightarrow{\sim} K_*\left( D^*(\Sigma \subseteq \overline{C},\Sigma)^\Gamma \right) \; .
  $$
  Observe that $P_R$ is in the image of $\mathrm{Ad}(V_R)$. Namely, it is the image of the projection onto the subspace of $L^2(\overline{C}_R)$ containing all functions $u(t,\cdot)=e^{-t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0$, $u_0 \in P_>H_\Sigma$, $t\in [0,R]$. Denote that projection by $P_R$ as well. Now, there is a homotopy of projections $P_R^s$, $s\in[0,1]$, where $P_R^s$ projects onto the subspace of $H_R$ containing all functions $u(t,\cdot)=e^{-(1-s)t\slashed{D}_\Sigma}u_0$, $u_0 \in\mathrm{im}(P_0)$. Then, $P_R^0=P_R$, while $P_R^1=V_\Sigma P_> V^*_\Sigma$. Because $V_\Sigma$ and $V_R$ induce isomorphisms, we conclude that
  $$
  [P_{\max}]=[P_R]= [P_>] \; \in \; K_*\left(D^*(\Sigma)^\Gamma \right) \cong K_*\left( D^*(\Sigma \subseteq \overline{C},\Sigma)^\Gamma \right) \; .
  $$
  Since we have already noted that the former projection represents $\mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_\Sigma(\slashed{D})$ and the latter $\rho^\Gamma(\slashed{D}_\Sigma)$, this concludes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Ad (i): We prove the claim for $\psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\Sigma_\infty}$, that for $\psi_{\Sigma_\infty} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\overline{\Omega}}$ then follows by taking the adjoint. Approximating $\chi$ by normalizing functions with compactly supported Fourier transforms, one may realize $\psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\Sigma_\infty}$ as the limit of finite-propagation operators supported near $\Sigma$. To see that $\psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\Sigma_\infty}$ is locally compact over $M\setminus \Sigma$, let $f\in C_0(M\setminus\Sigma)$. We may assume that $\mathrm{supp}(f)$ has some positive distance $\delta>0$ from $\Sigma$. For any normalizing function $\chi'$ with $\chi'(\slashed{D}_M)$ having propagation $<\delta$, it holds that $\left(\psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \chi'(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\Sigma_\infty}\right) f=0$. On the other hand, $\chi(\slashed{D}_M)$ and $\chi'(\slashed{D}_M)$ differ by an operator in $C^*(M)^\Gamma$, see e.g. \cite[Lemma 10.6.3]{HigsonRoe2000}. Thus $\left(\psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\Sigma_\infty}\right) f$ is compact. Analogously, $f\left(\psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \chi'(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\Sigma_\infty}\right)$ is also compact, whence we conclude $\psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\Sigma_\infty}\in D^*(\Sigma\subseteq M,\Sigma)^\Gamma$.

  Ad (ii): The K-homology class of $\psi_{\overline{\Omega}}\chi(\slashed{D}_M)\psi_{\overline{\Omega}}$ represents the image of $[\slashed{D}_M]$ under the map restriction map $K_0^\Gamma(M) \to K_0^\Gamma(\Omega)\cong K^\Gamma_0(\overline{\Omega},\Sigma)$. Hence, the claim follows from \cite[Prop.~10.8.8]{HigsonRoe2000}.

  Ad (iii): Analogously to (ii), $\psi_{\Sigma_\infty}\chi(\slashed{D}_M)\psi_{\Sigma_\infty}$ represents the class of $[\slashed{D}_{\Sigma_\infty}]$ in $K_0^\Gamma(\Sigma_\infty,\Sigma)$. Represent the latter by $\chi(\slashed{D}_{\Sigma_\infty,e})$ with $\slashed{D}_{\Sigma_\infty,e}$ the boundary condition \eqref{bc} for $\slashed{D}_{\Sigma_\infty}$. The operator $\chi(\slashed{D}_{\Sigma_\infty,e})$ is invertible modulo $D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\Sigma_\infty,\Sigma)^\Gamma$ by \cref{InvolutionModBdry}, hence it suffices to prove its difference from $\psi_{\Sigma_\infty}\chi(\slashed{D}_M)\psi_{\Sigma_\infty}$ to lie in $D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\Sigma_\infty,\Sigma)^\Gamma$. This can be done analogously to (i) by noting that modulo $D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\Sigma_\infty,\Sigma)^\Gamma$, we may replace $\chi$ by a normalizing function with compactly supported Fourier transform, which clearly leads to operators supported near $\Sigma$.

  Claim (iv) is proved entirely analogously to (iii).

title: Proof
body_md:
We focus on the proof of (ii). By \cref{decomp}(i) we may write
  $$
  \chi(\slashed{D}_M) = \begin{pmatrix}
  \psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\overline{\Omega}} & 0 \\ 0 & \psi_{\Sigma_\infty} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\Sigma_\infty}
  \end{pmatrix} \; \mathrm{mod} \; D^*(\Sigma\subseteq M , \Sigma)^\Gamma \; .
  $$
  Here, $\psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \in D^*(\overline{\Omega})^\Gamma$ is an involution modulo $D^*(\overline{\Omega},\Sigma)$, and $\psi_{\Sigma_\infty} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\Sigma_\infty} \in D^*(\Sigma_\infty)^\Gamma$ an involution modulo $D^*(\Sigma \subseteq \Sigma_\infty,\Sigma)^\Gamma$. Consider the commutative diagram\\
  \centerline{\xymatrix{
  K_{1}\left(\frac{D^*(\overline{\Omega})^\Gamma}{D^*(\overline{\Omega},\Sigma)^\Gamma}\right)\ar[d]_{\partial}\ar@{}[r]|{\oplus} & K_{1}\left(\frac{D^*(\Sigma_\infty)^\Gamma}{D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\Sigma_\infty,\Sigma)^\Gamma}\right)\ar[d]^{\partial} \ar[r] & K_{1}\left(\frac{D^*(M)^\Gamma}{D^*(\overline{\Omega}\subseteq M,\Sigma)^\Gamma}\right)\ar[d]^{\partial} \\
  K_{0}\left(D^*(\overline{\Omega},\Sigma)^\Gamma\right)\ar@{}[r]|{\oplus} & K_{0}\left(D^*(\Sigma\subseteq \Sigma_\infty,\Sigma)^\Gamma\right) \ar[r] & K_{0}\left(D^*(\overline{\Omega}\subseteq M,\Sigma)^\Gamma\right)
  }} 
  where the horizontal arrows are the sums of the respective inclusion maps. Note that the first vertical arrow is precisely the secondary uniform index map. Up to identifying $K_{0}(D^*(\Sigma\subseteq \Sigma_\infty,\Sigma)^\Gamma) \cong K_0(D^*(\Sigma)^\Gamma)$, the second is the index map $\mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_\Sigma$. The third vertical arrow maps the class of $\chi(\slashed{D}_M) \in D^*(M)^\Gamma$ to the image of $\mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_\mathrm{APS}(\slashed{D}_M)$ under the inclusion map $C^*(\overline{\Omega}\subseteq M) \hookrightarrow D^*(\overline{\Omega}\subseteq M,\Sigma)$. Moreover, we may identify $K_{0}\left(D^*(\overline{\Omega}\subseteq M,\Sigma)^\Gamma\right)$ with $K_{0}\left(D^*(\overline{\Omega},\Sigma)^\Gamma\right)$ by \cref{RelLocalized}. Appealing to \cref{decomp} (ii) and (iii), we thus find that
  $$
  \mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_\mathrm{APS}(\slashed{D}_M) = \mathrm{Ind}_\mathrm{sec}^\Gamma \left( \slashed{D}_\Omega \right) + \mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_\Sigma \left( \slashed{D}_{\Sigma_\infty} \right) \; ,
  $$
  To conclude the proof, we merely note that $\mathrm{Ind}^\Gamma_\Sigma( \slashed{D}_{\Sigma_\infty}) = - \rho^\Gamma(\slashed{D}_\Sigma)$ by \cref{FormulaCylinder}, where the sign comes from the fact that $\Sigma_\infty = (-\infty,0]\times\Sigma$ carries the opposite orientation from the cylinder $\overline{C}=[0,\infty) \times \Sigma$ considered in that lemma.

  By using that if $\overline{\Omega}$ has uniformly positive scalar curvature, $\psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \chi(\slashed{D}_M) \psi_{\overline{\Omega}} \in D^*(\overline{\Omega})^\Gamma$ is actually an involution modulo $D^*(\Sigma\subseteq\overline{\Omega},\Sigma)$, and appealing to \cref{decomp} (iv), claim (i) is proved entirely analogously.
